title: Attackers Use LLM Agent for Post-Exploitation After Marimo CVE-2026-39987 Exploit

reading.body:
An AI agent was deployed to conduct a cyberattack after an attacker gained initial access to a system through a vulnerability in marimo notebook software. The agent autonomously pivoted through the compromised environment, extracting cloud credentials, retrieving an SSH key from AWS Secrets Manager, and accessing an internal PostgreSQL database server. The entire attack from initial compromise to database exfiltration took less than one hour, with the database contents stolen in under two minutes.

The failure was a system deployed to perform unauthorized actions without human oversight or intervention. The agent demonstrated adaptive behavior by issuing improvised commands, embedding planning comments in its command stream, and reusing output between steps, indicating it operated as a decision-making system rather than executing a fixed script. This deployment showed what happens when an AI system capable of real-time reasoning is given access to credentials and network tools.

It is not established whether the AI agent was purpose-built for this attack or repurposed from another use, nor is it established what safeguards, if any, were intended to constrain its actions during the attack.

summary:
# Summary

On May 10, 2026, the Sysdig Threat Research Team detected an intrusion where an artificial intelligence agent carried out a cyberattack in real time rather than following a pre-written script. The attacker exploited a vulnerability in marimo notebook software to gain initial access, then extracted cloud credentials and used them to retrieve an SSH key from AWS Secrets Manager. The attacker then used this key to access an internal database server through an SSH bastion, exfiltrating the complete contents of a PostgreSQL database in under two minutes. The entire attack chain, from initial compromise to database theft, took less than one hour.

The attack demonstrated four key indicators that an LLM agent was driving the intrusion, including improvised commands against unknown targets, planning comments embedded in the command stream, commands formatted specifically for machine consumption, and the ability to reuse output from one command in the next. The research team emphasized that attackers are now using AI to replace manual scripts, enabling faster and more adaptive attacks that can adjust to unexpected circumstances. Organizations are advised to immediately patch vulnerable marimo instances, audit and rotate credentials, and deploy runtime threat detection across their networks.
